nameStory: Common purslane gets its name from the Old French 'porcelaine,' referring to its thick, porcelain-like succulent leaves. The 'common' part distinguishes it from its showier cousin, the moss rose, which is often grown in gardens for its bright flowers.
description: Common purslane is a low-growing, mat-forming succulent that spreads along the ground in a circular pattern. This fleshy annual plant rarely grows taller than 6 inches but can spread up to 2 feet across. Its thick, paddle-shaped leaves store water like a tiny cactus, and it produces small yellow flowers that open only in sunny conditions. You'll often find it growing in sidewalk cracks, garden paths, and disturbed soil.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy leaves shaped like tiny paddles or teardrops, smooth to the touch and often with a waxy feel. They're typically green but may have reddish edges, especially in sunny spots.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinctive circular mats that radiate outward from a central taproot, with reddish stems that lie flat against the ground and feel succulent when squeezed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow flowers with 5 petals that only open in bright sunshine, usually in the morning. They're small enough that you might miss them at first glance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish or purplish stems that are thick and juicy, breaking with a satisfying snap when bent. No hairs or thorns anywhere on the plant.

habitat: Thrives in disturbed, compacted soils where other plants struggle, especially in full sun. You'll commonly spot it in sidewalk cracks, garden paths, driveways, vacant lots, and along roadsides throughout New England. It particularly loves areas with poor, sandy, or gravelly soil that drains quickly.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate when soil warms in late spring, starting as tiny rosettes of succulent leaves. Young plants are most tender and easily identified by their distinctive circular growth pattern.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when plants form large mats and produce their small yellow flowers. This is when the succulent leaves are most pronounced and the reddish stems are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue growing until first frost, often producing seeds in small capsules. The fleshy leaves may take on more reddish coloration as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die with hard frost, leaving behind seeds that will germinate the following spring. No above-ground parts survive New England winters.

funFact: This humble 'weed' is actually a nutritional powerhouse that contains more omega-3 fatty acids than most fish, plus it's been eaten as a delicacy in Mediterranean cuisine for thousands of years—Mahatma Gandhi called it one of his favorite foods!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other low-growing weeds like chickweed or spurge, but purslane's thick, succulent leaves are unmistakable once you feel them—they're plump and fleshy like a tiny jade plant, while look-alikes have thin, papery leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being considered a troublesome weed by many gardeners, purslane is entirely edible and highly nutritious. It's been cultivated as a food crop in many parts of the world and is sometimes called 'verdolaga' in Mexican markets or 'portulak' in European contexts.
compareHints: Unlike its ornamental relative moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora), common purslane has much smaller, less showy yellow flowers and forms flat mats rather than upright mounds. Moss rose is typically grown in gardens and has larger, more colorful flowers in shades of pink, red, white, or orange that are much more noticeable than purslane's tiny yellow blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its weedy cousin common purslane (which has flat, paddle-shaped leaves and tiny yellow flowers), moss rose has cylindrical needle-like leaves and large, showy flowers in many colors.
